nature-eecon-019.title: Material flow analysis: following matter through a system
nature-eecon-019.text:
Matter is never created or destroyed, so every tonne entering a system must leave it or pile up inside. Material flow analysis builds on that fact. It is a method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system, and a core method of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}.

It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter. Every analysis has a boundary, processes, flows between them and stocks within them. Unlike economic accounting, it also tracks waste, emissions and natural resources that have no market. It can cover a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life or a whole national economy. The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.

nature-eecon-009.title: The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources
nature-eecon-009.text:
Crops, forests, fish, animals and micro-organisms supply the bioeconomy. It is the part of the economy that uses {{ref:nature-res-212}} from land and sea, plus biotechnology, to produce food, materials, products and energy. Its products include food, feed, bio-based products, bioenergy and services based on biological resources.

Its aims are to secure food, use {{ref:nature-res-248}} more sustainably and reduce dependence on fossil resources and minerals. The term became popular from the mid-2000s, when the EU and OECD adopted it as a policy framework; the OECD (2006) and EU (2012) created bioeconomy strategies.

Not everyone is persuaded. Critics fear its 'green growth' framing keeps an unsustainable model in place, and may turn living things into economic commodities. Whether it changes the economy or merely sustains it is disputed.

nature-eecon-041.title: Collecting recyclables: curbside, drop-off and buy-back
nature-eecon-041.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} starts with collection, and there are three main ways to gather recyclables from the waste stream: drop-off centers, buy-back centers and curbside collection. Each trades public convenience against government ease and expense. Buy-back centers pay for cleaned, sorted recyclables, a clear incentive. Drop-off centers are easiest to set up but handle low, unpredictable amounts. Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection, gives the purest recycled material.

nature-eecon-042.title: Recycling policy: securing supply and creating demand
nature-eecon-042.text: Recycling needs a steady supply of material and buyers for what it makes. Recycling supply and demand policies are laws that secure both. Supply comes from mandatory collection, container deposit laws and bans on throwing certain things away. Demand is raised by minimum recycled-content mandates, utilization rates, government purchasing policies and labels on recycled products. Together they help build a {{ref:nature-econ-342}} for recycled goods.

nature-eecon-039.title: Types of recycling: mechanical, chemical, closed and open loop
nature-eecon-039.text: Not all {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} is the same. Sorted by process, mechanical recycling shreds, melts and reforms materials, while chemical recycling breaks them into their chemical components. Sorted by outcome, closed-loop recycling makes the same product without significant loss of quality. Open-loop recycling makes different, often lower-quality products. Closed-loop recycling is generally seen as more sustainable, because it loses fewer resources along the way.

nature-eecon-010.title: The circular bioeconomy: biology meets the closed loop
nature-eecon-010.text: According to the European Commission's science service, the circular bioeconomy produces €1.5 trillion in value added, 11% of EU GDP. It is a {{ref:nature-eecon-009}} run on circular principles. It produces food, materials and energy from renewable biological resources while reducing dependence on other natural resources. One study found it may be necessary for a carbon-neutral future in line with the Paris Agreement.

nature-eecon-005.title: Circular economy standards: rules for going circular
nature-eecon-005.text: In 2017 the British Standards Institution launched BS 8001:2017, the first circular economy standard. Such standards are formal guides that help organizations apply circular economy principles. The international body ISO followed, setting up technical committee TC 323 in 2018. In 2024 and 2025 it published four ISO 59000-series standards, including ISO 59020 on measuring circularity performance.

nature-eecon-006.title: The EU Circular Economy Action Plan
nature-eecon-006.text: The European Union has a policy program for moving its economy toward circularity: the Circular Economy Action Plan. The first plan, 'Closing the loop', had 54 measures aimed at competitiveness, growth and jobs. The European Commission adopted a new plan in March 2020. It targets resource-hungry industries, waste reduction and decarbonization, the cutting of carbon emissions, and it makes sustainable products the standard.

nature-eecon-031.title: Pay as you throw: a bill for every bag
nature-eecon-031.text:
In Ferrara, Italy, waste fell by 30% overall and recycling rose by 40% once households paid by the bag. Pay as you throw charges households for rubbish collection according to how much waste they put out, instead of a flat fee. Under a flat rate or tax, everyone pays the same, so there is no {{ref:nature-econ-089}} to throw away less.

The scheme rests on the {{ref:nature-pol-095}} and on shared responsibility. Waste can be measured by weight, size, or counts of special bags, tags or containers. Recycling and composting are often collected free, which nudges people toward them. In North America, it cut residential waste by 9-38% and raised recycling by 6-40%. There is a catch: charging for waste can lead to illegal dumping, known as 'fly-tipping'.

nature-eecon-036.title: Product-service systems: selling light, not light bulbs
nature-eecon-036.text:
Philips sells some customers a promised level of light, not lamps. They pay per lux. A product-service system is a business model in which a firm sells a combined package of {{ref:nature-econ-122}} that together meet a customer's need. Customers want the function a product provides, not necessarily to own it, so firms may be paid per unit of service. Xerox's pay-per-copy model works the same way.

Research names three classes. In product-oriented systems, ownership passes to the customer with added services. In use-oriented ones, the provider keeps ownership and sells use through sharing, pooling or leasing. In result-oriented ones, services replace products. The concept was first developed at the Politecnico di Milano between 1993 and 1996. Not every such system cuts material use, but some authors claim they can improve {{ref:nature-eecon-027}} by a factor of 4 or more.

nature-eecon-026.title: Biorefineries: an oil refinery for plants
nature-eecon-026.text:
The pulp and paper industry is considered the first industrialized biorefinery system. A biorefinery is a facility that converts biomass, material from living things, into energy and other useful products such as chemicals. The IEA defines biorefining as sustainable processing of biomass into food, feed, chemicals, materials and bioenergy, the full product range of the {{ref:nature-eecon-009}}.

It works like an oil refinery. Biomass is split into intermediates such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Each refining step is called a cascading phase. Systems are classified by platform, product, feedstock and conversion process, which may be mechanical, biochemical, chemical or thermochemical.

The goals are broad: supplying fuels and chemicals, creating rural jobs, getting value from waste and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Biobased does not automatically mean harmless. Growing the biomass can still cause land-use change, pesticide pollution and eutrophication, the overloading of water with nutrients. So life cycle assessment is used to compare biobased products with conventional ones.

nature-eecon-048.title: Repurposing: giving junk a new job
nature-eecon-048.text: An old tyre can become a boat fender, and a drum can become a feeding trough or compost bin. Repurposing means using an item for a purpose other than the one it was made for, usually something considered junk. It is a form of {{ref:nature-pol-066}}. Earthship houses take it furthest, using tyres as insulating walls and bottles as glass walls.

nature-eecon-049.title: Right to repair: who gets to fix your phone
nature-eecon-049.text:
Broken and used electronics became the fastest-growing waste stream as smartphones and computers spread. The right to repair is the legal right of owners to maintain, repair or modify their own devices and equipment, such as cars, electronics and farm machinery.

The obstacles are deliberate. Manufacturer-only servicing, restricted parts and tools, and software locks create a 'repair monopoly', a form of {{ref:nature-econ-349}}. Such monopolies have been found to raise prices, cause delays and reduce consumer choice. The movement aims to favor repair over replacement and to make repairs cheaper, supporting a more sustainable economy with less electronic waste. The EU adopted its Right to Repair Directive on 30 May 2024. Canada became the first country with a national right-to-repair law on 7 November 2024.

nature-eecon-033.title: Microplastics: the plastic too small to see
nature-eecon-033.text: By 2050 the weight of microplastics in the sea is estimated to exceed that of fish. Microplastics are tiny insoluble plastic particles, from 1 micrometre to 5 mm across, that pollute water, soil and air. Primary ones, such as microbeads, clothing microfibers and pellets, are already small when released. Secondary ones come from larger items breaking down. Because some plastics take hundreds to thousands of years to degrade, these particles are likely to be eaten and build up in living things.

nature-eecon-046.title: Composting and digestion: letting microbes recycle food
nature-eecon-046.text: Food scraps and garden waste can become compost, fertilizer and energy. Composting and anaerobic digestion are biological processes that break down such organic waste; digestion works without oxygen. Methane from digestion can be captured to generate electricity and heat. Anaerobic digestion of the organic part of municipal waste has been found more environmentally effective than landfill, incineration or pyrolysis, the breaking down of waste by heat. It is a clear case of {{ref:nature-eecon-044}}.

nature-eecon-045.title: Mining sewage: recovering resources from wastewater
nature-eecon-045.text: Sewers were first built only to carry waste away. Since the 1970s the focus moved to cleaning water, and since about 2003 to recovering resources. Resource recovery from wastewater wins back water, energy, nutrients and other materials from wastewater, sewage sludge and human excreta. Nutrients from these sources are widely reused in farming, often unsafely. WHO guidelines from 2006 set a framework for doing it safely.

nature-eecon-058.title: The Zero Waste Hierarchy: from best use to last resort
nature-eecon-058.text: The Zero Waste Hierarchy ranks policies and strategies for a {{ref:nature-eecon-057}} system, from the highest and best use of materials down to the lowest. It adds depth to the familiar 3Rs of reduce, reuse and recycle. It also steers policy and investment toward the top of the ranking. It is meant for everyone from policymakers to industry and individuals, and it helps them judge proposed solutions.

nature-eecon-016.title: Cradle to Cradle certification: grading products by their materials
nature-eecon-016.text: The Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute runs a certification that scores products against {{ref:nature-eecon-013}} criteria. One criterion is material health, which identifies the chemicals in a product. Another is material reutilization, which covers recovery and recycling at end of life. Materials are ranked green for low risk, yellow for acceptable, red for those to be phased out, and grey where data are incomplete.

nature-eecon-015.title: Downcycling: each round a little worse
nature-eecon-015.text: A plastic computer case might become a plastic cup, then a park bench, and finally plastic waste. That slide is downcycling: reusing materials to make products of lower quality or value than the original. It is the common fate of much {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. Cradle-to-cradle design aims to stop it, keeping technical materials cycling at full quality instead.

nature-eecon-014.title: Technical and biological nutrients: two loops, not one
nature-eecon-014.text: Cradle-to-cradle design splits all materials into two kinds. Technical nutrients are non-toxic synthetic materials, such as plastics and metals, that cycle in industry and can be used again and again without losing quality. Biological nutrients are organic materials that decompose into soil and feed small life forms without harming the environment. In a hypothetical cradle-to-cradle shoe, the sole is a biological nutrient and the upper a technical one, separated when the shoe is returned.
